description: Tuscan city-republic (c. 1125–1555) whose banking firms, the Gran Tavola of the Bonsignori, financed the papacy before Florence's Medici replaced them; the Black Death (1348) killed half the population and broke Siena's commercial primacy, while the Lorenzetti fresco Allegory of Good and Bad Government in the Palazzo Pubblico remains the most sophisticated medieval visual statement of civic republican ideology.

geographic.notes: Centroid approximate; polygon pending schematic or OHM sourcing.

lifecycle_phases.description: Commune established; emerging rivalry with Florence.
Banking and pilgrimage economy grows; republic expands territory.
Council of Nine; Duccio and Lorenzetti; height of Sienese culture and commerce.
Black Death collapses population and banking.
Florentine and imperial pressure; republic weakens.

rise_factors.description: Siena lay on the Via Francigena pilgrimage route and its bankers acted as papal financial agents, making it a major European banking center.
Sienese merchant networks in France and England, combined with Monte dei Paschi banking, generated extraordinary wealth.
The Council of Nine (1287–1355) was a sophisticated oligarchic civic government managing urban finances effectively.
Sienese banking houses, Bonsignori, Tolomei, Piccolomini, held the papal banking account for decades in the 13th century, accumulating vast wealth from loans to popes, emperors, and European kings.

The Sienese school of painting under Duccio, Simone Martini, and the Lorenzetti brothers produced Italy's finest Gothic sacred art, and Lorenzetti's Allegory of Good and Bad Government became the defining image of communal self-governance.

decline_factors.description: Black Death 1348 killed roughly half of Siena's population, permanently devastating its banking networks and urban economy.
Florentine and later Spanish Habsburg pressure progressively constrained Sienese independence through the 15th century.
Factional politics (Nine vs Twelve) created endemic civic instability after the fall of the Nine in 1355.
Siena lost approximately 50–60% of its population to the Black Death of 1348, more severely than most Italian cities, permanently reducing its commercial and military capacity relative to Florence.
Imperial forces besieged and conquered Siena in 1555 after a heroic three-year siege; Charles V ceded it to his son Philip II, and it was subsequently assigned to Cosimo I de' Medici of Tuscany.

sources.author: Wickham, Chris
